name: Core Concepts Drill
desc: Short concept checks on the rules the exam keeps testing: loop control, enforcement in code, subagent context, structured output. A warm-up before the mocks.
source: Written for the CCA Foundations Prep artifact.

questions.q: The agent’s loop exits when the assistant’s reply contains the word “resolved”. Some conversations end while a tool call is still pending. What should control the loop?
options: Continue while stop_reason is tool_use and exit on end_turn
Match a longer, more specific completion phrase
Stop after a fixed ten iterations
Tell the model to end every final reply with a special token
questions.explain:
The API already reports whether Claude wants tools run. Text matching and fixed caps are the two named anti-patterns for loop control.
Not “Match a longer, more specific completion phrase” — Still text matching: a change of phrasing, or the phrase appearing mid-task, breaks it, and it ignores what the API already reports.
Not “Stop after a fixed ten iterations” — A fixed cap cuts off unfinished tasks and wastes turns on finished ones. A cap is a safety net, not the stop signal.
Not “Tell the model to end every final reply with a special token” — It relies on the model always emitting the token, which is only probable. stop_reason is set by the API on every response.

questions.q: The synthesis subagent writes a report that ignores what the web research subagent found. Its prompt reads “Synthesise the research on battery recycling”. What is the fix?
options: Include the research subagent’s full findings in the synthesis prompt
Raise the synthesis subagent’s max_tokens
Add “use earlier findings” to the synthesis system prompt
Let the two subagents exchange messages directly
questions.explain:
Subagents have isolated context and inherit nothing. The coordinator must pass prior output explicitly; direct subagent traffic breaks hub-and-spoke.
Not “Raise the synthesis subagent’s max_tokens” — max_tokens limits output length. It cannot supply findings the subagent never received.
Not “Add “use earlier findings” to the synthesis system prompt” — There are no earlier findings in its context to use. A subagent starts with only what its prompt contains.
Not “Let the two subagents exchange messages directly” — Direct subagent-to-subagent traffic bypasses the coordinator, which loses observability and central error handling.

questions.q: Three independent subtopics are researched one after another and the run is slow. What speeds it up with the least change?
options: Have the coordinator issue three Task calls in one response
Merge the three subtopics into one subagent prompt
Let each subagent spawn the next when it finishes
Move the coordinator to a larger model
questions.explain:
Several Task calls in a single coordinator turn run concurrently. Merging loses focus and chaining keeps it sequential.
Not “Merge the three subtopics into one subagent prompt” — One subagent covering three topics still works through them in sequence and loses focus on each.
Not “Let each subagent spawn the next when it finishes” — Chaining keeps the work sequential and moves routing out of the coordinator.
Not “Move the coordinator to a larger model” — A larger model does not make sequential calls run concurrently.

questions.q: A report on “AI in creative industries” covers visual art thoroughly and says nothing about music or writing. Every subagent completed successfully. Where is the root cause?
options: The coordinator decomposed the topic too narrowly
The search subagent used weak queries
The synthesis subagent dropped sections
The report subagent’s output limit was too low
questions.explain:
If subagents succeeded on what they were given, the gap is in what was assigned. Narrow decomposition is a coordinator failure.
Not “The search subagent used weak queries” — The search subagent was never asked about music or writing, so its queries are not where the gap is.
Not “The synthesis subagent dropped sections” — Synthesis can only drop what it received. Nothing on those subtopics was ever gathered.
Not “The report subagent’s output limit was too low” — A length limit would truncate the report. It would not remove whole subject areas while keeping one in depth.

questions.q: Subagents are defined correctly, but the coordinator never delegates and tries to do all the work itself. What is the most likely configuration gap?
options: Task is missing from the coordinator’s allowedTools
The subagents lack a tool_choice setting
The coordinator has no PostToolUse hook
The subagent descriptions are too long
questions.explain:
Task is the tool that spawns subagents. Without it in allowedTools the coordinator cannot delegate.
Not “The subagents lack a tool_choice setting” — tool_choice controls whether a tool must be called on a request. It does not give the coordinator a way to spawn subagents.
Not “The coordinator has no PostToolUse hook” — PostToolUse hooks process tool results. They play no part in delegation.
Not “The subagent descriptions are too long” — Long descriptions cost tokens but do not block delegation. Without Task the coordinator cannot call any subagent at all.

questions.q: Policy says refunds above $500 must never be issued without human approval. The system prompt states this, yet 2% of large refunds still go through. What closes the gap?
options: A hook that intercepts process_refund, blocks amounts above $500 and routes to escalation
Restating the rule in capitals at the top of the prompt
Few-shot examples of declining large refunds
A nightly audit that flags large refunds for review
questions.explain:
“Must never” needs a deterministic guarantee. Prompt changes only raise the probability, and an audit finds the breach after the money has gone.
Not “Restating the rule in capitals at the top of the prompt” — Emphasis raises compliance but cannot make it certain, and the rule says never.
Not “Few-shot examples of declining large refunds” — Examples improve the odds, not the guarantee. Some large refunds would still go through.
Not “A nightly audit that flags large refunds for review” — An audit finds the breach after the refund has been paid. It detects; it does not prevent.

questions.q: Three MCP tools return dates as Unix timestamps, ISO 8601 strings and “3 Mar 2025”. The agent sometimes miscompares them. What is the cleanest fix?
options: A PostToolUse hook that normalises dates before the model sees the result
A prompt section explaining each tool’s date format
A date-conversion tool the model can call when needed
A larger context window so more examples fit
questions.explain:
Normalising in a hook is deterministic and costs the model nothing. The other options leave the conversion to the model’s judgement each time.
Not “A prompt section explaining each tool’s date format” — The model still has to convert correctly every time, so the errors continue at a lower rate.
Not “A date-conversion tool the model can call when needed” — The model must remember to call it for every date, which adds turns and can be skipped.
Not “A larger context window so more examples fit” — Context size is not the problem. The model has the dates and miscompares the formats.

questions.q: You ask an agent to raise test coverage in a large legacy codebase nobody on the team knows. Which decomposition suits this?
options: Map the structure first, then build a prioritised plan that adapts to what is found
A fixed pipeline that runs the same five steps on every module
One prompt that asks for tests for the whole repository
Work through the directories in alphabetical order
questions.explain:
Open-ended work in unknown territory calls for dynamic decomposition. Fixed pipelines fit predictable, repeatable tasks.
Not “A fixed pipeline that runs the same five steps on every module” — A fixed pipeline assumes the steps are known in advance. Here the structure is unknown and modules differ.
Not “One prompt that asks for tests for the whole repository” — One prompt for the whole repository dilutes attention and overruns the context window.
Not “Work through the directories in alphabetical order” — Alphabetical order ignores risk and value, so critical untested code may come last.

questions.q: Yesterday a named session traced a bug through the payments module. Overnight a colleague refactored that module. How should you continue today?
options: Start a new session with a structured summary of yesterday’s findings
Resume the session and carry on from the last message
Fork yesterday’s session and continue in the fork
Resume the session and run /compact first
questions.explain:
The old tool results describe code that no longer exists. A fresh session with a summary is more reliable than resuming on stale context; forking and compacting keep the stale results.
Not “Resume the session and carry on from the last message” — The session’s tool results describe the code before the refactor, so the agent would reason from files that no longer match.
Not “Fork yesterday’s session and continue in the fork” — A fork inherits the same stale context up to the branch point.
Not “Resume the session and run /compact first” — Compacting shortens the stale history. It does not make it current.

questions.q: get_customer and lookup_order each have a one-line description, and the agent often calls the wrong one. What is the most effective first step?
options: Expand both descriptions with input formats, example queries and when not to use each
Put a routing classifier in front of the agent
Merge the two tools into one
Add few-shot examples to the system prompt
questions.explain:
Descriptions are the primary selection signal and the cheapest fix. A classifier is over-engineering; few-shot adds tokens without fixing the cause.
Not “Put a routing classifier in front of the agent” — A classifier is new infrastructure for a problem the descriptions cause. It is not a proportionate first step.
Not “Merge the two tools into one” — The tools do different jobs. Merging gives one broader, vaguer tool and takes more rework than fixing two descriptions.
Not “Add few-shot examples to the system prompt” — Few-shot adds tokens and works around weak descriptions instead of fixing them. It is the next step only if clear descriptions are not enough.

questions.q: An MCP tool returns “Operation failed” for every problem. The agent keeps retrying refunds that break policy. What should the tool return?
options: isError: true with an error category, a retryable flag and a clear message
An empty success response so the agent moves on
The same message with a retry limit stated in the prompt
An exception that ends the conversation
questions.explain:
The agent needs to know a business-rule violation is not retryable. Generic errors prevent any sensible recovery decision.
Not “An empty success response so the agent moves on” — Reporting success for a failed refund misleads both the agent and the customer.
Not “The same message with a retry limit stated in the prompt” — A retry cap limits the damage, but the agent still cannot tell a policy block from a timeout.
Not “An exception that ends the conversation” — Ending the conversation abandons the customer when the agent could explain the policy or escalate.

questions.q: The search subagent returns an empty list both when nothing matches and when the search service times out. The coordinator then reports “no evidence exists”. What needs to change?
options: Return a structured error for the timeout and keep the empty list for genuine no-match
Have the coordinator always run every search twice
Return a placeholder result on timeout
Tell the coordinator to treat empty lists with caution
questions.explain:
An access failure and a valid empty result mean different things. Collapsing them hides the fact that the answer is unknown.
Not “Have the coordinator always run every search twice” — Doubling every search wastes calls and still cannot tell a second timeout from a genuine no-match.
Not “Return a placeholder result on timeout” — A placeholder is fabricated data that could end up in the report.
Not “Tell the coordinator to treat empty lists with caution” — The coordinator has nothing to be cautious about: both cases look identical until the subagent reports them differently.

questions.q: The synthesis subagent has 18 tools, including web search, and keeps running its own poor searches instead of using the findings it was given. What is the best fix?
options: Restrict it to the few tools its role needs
Add “do not search the web” to its prompt
Rewrite all 18 tool descriptions
Give it a larger model
questions.explain:
Too many tools lowers selection reliability, and agents misuse tools outside their role. Scoping the toolset removes the option entirely.
Not “Add “do not search the web” to its prompt” — A prompt instruction is only probably followed, and the tool is still there to be called.
Not “Rewrite all 18 tool descriptions” — Better descriptions help choose among relevant tools. Web search is not relevant to this role at all.
Not “Give it a larger model” — The problem is the toolset, not capability. A larger model with the same 18 tools can still misuse them.

questions.q: The whole team needs the same GitHub MCP server, and each developer has their own token. How should it be configured?
options: In project .mcp.json, committed, with the token as ${GITHUB_TOKEN}
Each developer adds it to ~/.claude.json
In .mcp.json with a shared token written in the file
Described in the project CLAUDE.md
questions.explain:
Project scope shares the server through git; environment variable expansion keeps secrets out of the file. User scope is for personal servers.
Not “Each developer adds it to ~/.claude.json” — User scope is not shared, so every developer sets it up by hand and configurations drift.
Not “In .mcp.json with a shared token written in the file” — A token committed to git is a leaked secret, and everyone would act under one identity.
Not “Described in the project CLAUDE.md” — CLAUDE.md holds instructions. MCP servers are configured in .mcp.json.

questions.q: You need to find where the error message “Invalid session token” is raised in an unfamiliar repository. Which built-in tool comes first?
options: Grep
Glob
Read on each file in src/
Edit
questions.explain:
Grep searches file contents. Glob matches file names, and reading every file burns context.
Not “Glob” — Glob matches file names and paths, not text inside files.
Not “Read on each file in src/” — Reading every file floods the context when one search would find the line.
Not “Edit” — Edit changes a file you have already located. It does not search.

questions.q: A new joiner’s Claude Code ignores naming conventions that work for a senior developer. The conventions are in the senior’s ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md. What fixes this for the team?
options: Move them to the project CLAUDE.md and commit it
Ask the joiner to copy the file into their home directory
Put them in a slash command everyone runs at session start
Add them to .mcp.json
questions.explain:
User-level memory applies to one person and is not shared through version control. Team standards belong at project level.
Not “Ask the joiner to copy the file into their home directory” — Copies drift, and every future joiner has to repeat the step. The standard should travel with the repository.
Not “Put them in a slash command everyone runs at session start” — It depends on everyone remembering to run it. Project CLAUDE.md loads automatically.
Not “Add them to .mcp.json” — .mcp.json configures MCP servers, not coding conventions.

questions.q: Testing conventions should apply to every *.test.tsx file, and those files are spread across forty directories. What is the best setup?
options: A .claude/rules/ file with paths: ["**/*.test.tsx"] in its frontmatter
A CLAUDE.md in each of the forty directories
A longer root CLAUDE.md with a testing section
A /test-rules command developers run before editing tests
questions.explain:
Path-scoped rules follow the file type wherever it lives and load only when relevant. Directory files would mean forty copies; the root file loads the rules always.
Not “A CLAUDE.md in each of the forty directories” — That is forty copies to maintain, and a test file in a new directory gets none.
Not “A longer root CLAUDE.md with a testing section” — It works, but the testing rules then load in every session, even when no test file is touched.
Not “A /test-rules command developers run before editing tests” — It relies on developers remembering to run it. Path rules load automatically.

questions.q: A codebase-analysis skill prints thousands of lines and leaves the main session short of context. Which SKILL.md setting addresses this?
options: context: fork
allowed-tools
argument-hint
Moving the skill to ~/.claude/skills/
questions.explain:
context: fork runs the skill in an isolated subagent context, so only its result returns to the main session.
Not “allowed-tools” — allowed-tools restricts which tools the skill may use. Its output still lands in the main session.
Not “argument-hint” — argument-hint only prompts for parameters. It has no effect on context.
Not “Moving the skill to ~/.claude/skills/” — That changes who can use the skill, not where its output goes.

questions.q: You are replacing the authentication library in a monolith. About 45 files change and there are at least three workable designs. How should you start?
options: In planning mode, exploring and agreeing an approach before any edits
Direct execution, one file at a time
Direct execution with a very detailed prompt
Ask for a single diff covering all 45 files
questions.explain:
Scale, architectural consequences and several viable approaches are the signals for planning mode. Direct execution suits small, well-understood changes.
Not “Direct execution, one file at a time” — Editing file by file commits to one approach before the three designs have been compared.
Not “Direct execution with a very detailed prompt” — A detailed prompt still skips exploring the codebase and choosing between designs before edits begin.
Not “Ask for a single diff covering all 45 files” — A single 45-file diff cannot be reviewed properly and still skips the design decision.

questions.q: A pipeline step runs claude "Review this pull request" and hangs until the job times out. What is wrong?
options: It needs -p to run non-interactively
It needs --output-format json
It needs a longer job timeout
It needs --resume with the previous session
questions.explain:
Without -p Claude Code waits for interactive input. Print mode processes the prompt, writes to stdout and exits.
Not “It needs --output-format json” — It changes the output format, but without -p the session is still interactive and waits for input.
Not “It needs a longer job timeout” — The job would wait just as long. The process never exits on its own.
Not “It needs --resume with the previous session” — Resuming is still interactive, and a CI job has no earlier session to resume.

questions.q: The review job must post inline comments on the pull request automatically. Which output setup supports that?
options: --output-format json with --json-schema describing file, line and comment
Plain text output parsed with regular expressions
A prompt asking for a Markdown table
Streaming output read line by line
questions.explain:
Schema-validated JSON is reliably parseable. Parsing free text is fragile.
Not “Plain text output parsed with regular expressions” — Free text changes shape between runs, so regular expressions break.
Not “A prompt asking for a Markdown table” — A Markdown table is still unvalidated text that has to be parsed.
Not “Streaming output read line by line” — Streaming changes how output is delivered, not its structure. Each line is still free text.

questions.q: Each new push triggers a full review and the same comments are posted again. What is the right fix?
options: Pass the prior review results and ask only for new or unresolved issues
Review only the first commit of each pull request
Lower the temperature so the output is stable
Post all findings as one summary comment
questions.explain:
Giving the reviewer its earlier findings lets it report only what changed. The other options hide the duplication or skip later commits.
Not “Review only the first commit of each pull request” — Later commits would go unreviewed.
Not “Lower the temperature so the output is stable” — Lower temperature makes output more repeatable, which means the same comments again.
Not “Post all findings as one summary comment” — The same findings are still repeated on each push, only inside one comment.

questions.q: The reviewer flags so many style nits that developers have started ignoring its real bug reports. What should change first?
options: Define what to report and what to ignore, with severity levels and examples
Add “be more conservative” to the prompt
Only post findings the model rates 8/10 or higher
Switch to a larger model
questions.explain:
Explicit categorical criteria outperform vague caution. False positives in one category destroy trust in all, and self-rated confidence is unreliable.
Not “Add “be more conservative” to the prompt” — Vague guidance gives the model no boundary between a nit and a bug, so behaviour barely changes.
Not “Only post findings the model rates 8/10 or higher” — Self-rated confidence is poorly calibrated. The model can be confidently wrong about a style nit.
Not “Switch to a larger model” — The model is doing what the prompt allows. A larger one would flag the same categories.

questions.q: Extraction instructions are already detailed, yet output format still varies between invoice layouts. What is the most effective addition?
options: Two to four examples showing correct extraction from different layouts
A longer description of the expected format
A second model call that reformats the output
Lower temperature
questions.explain:
Few-shot examples are the strongest lever for consistent format and help the model generalise across document structures.
Not “A longer description of the expected format” — The instructions are already detailed. More prose has little left to give where examples show the target directly.
Not “A second model call that reformats the output” — A reformatting pass doubles the cost and can introduce its own errors. It treats the symptom.
Not “Lower temperature” — Temperature reduces randomness on the same input. The variation here comes from different layouts.

questions.q: The prompt says “respond only in JSON”, and 3% of responses fail to parse. What is the most reliable fix?
options: Define an extraction tool with a JSON Schema and read the tool_use input
Write “ONLY JSON, no other text” in capitals
Repair malformed JSON with regular expressions
Retry until the response parses
questions.explain:
Tool use with a schema removes syntax errors at the source. The alternatives patch the symptom.
Not “Write “ONLY JSON, no other text” in capitals” — Stronger wording lowers the failure rate but cannot guarantee valid JSON.
Not “Repair malformed JSON with regular expressions” — Repairing malformed output is fragile and can silently change values.
Not “Retry until the response parses” — Retries add cost and latency, and the next attempt can fail the same way.

questions.q: Extraction now uses tool_use with a strict schema. Output always parses, but in some invoices the line items do not add up to the total. What addresses this?
options: Extract calculated_total and stated_total, compare them, and retry with the specific discrepancy
Tighten the schema further
Mark the total field as required
Force the tool with tool_choice
questions.explain:
Schemas guarantee structure, not meaning. Semantic errors need validation logic and a feedback loop.
Not “Tighten the schema further” — A schema checks types and structure. It cannot express that line items must add up to the total.
Not “Mark the total field as required” — The total is already present. The problem is that it is inconsistent, not missing.
Not “Force the tool with tool_choice” — Forcing the tool guarantees the call is made, not that the numbers inside it agree.

questions.q: contract_end_date is a required field. Some contracts have no end date, and the model fills in plausible ones. What is the best schema change?
options: Make the field nullable so the model can report that it is absent
Add “do not invent dates” to the prompt
Add a validation retry when the date looks wrong
Add few-shot examples of date formats
questions.explain:
A required field forces a value. Allowing null removes the pressure to fabricate.
Not “Add “do not invent dates” to the prompt” — The schema still demands a value, so the instruction and the schema conflict and the schema wins.
Not “Add a validation retry when the date looks wrong” — A plausible invented date passes validation, so there is nothing for the retry to catch.
Not “Add few-shot examples of date formats” — Format examples show how to write a date, not what to do when there is none.

questions.q: Validation fails because the warranty period is missing. It appears only in an annex that was not provided. What should the pipeline do?
options: Route the item for the missing document or human review; a retry cannot help
Retry up to three times with the validation error
Retry with a larger model
Ask the model to estimate from similar contracts
questions.explain:
Retry-with-feedback corrects mistakes on information that is present. It cannot produce information absent from the source.
Not “Retry up to three times with the validation error” — Each retry re-reads the same document, and the value is not in it.
Not “Retry with a larger model” — No model can read a document it was not given.
Not “Ask the model to estimate from similar contracts” — An estimate is fabricated data presented as if it were extracted.

questions.q: You run two jobs: a pre-merge check on each pull request and a nightly technical-debt report across 8,000 files. Which should use the Message Batches API?
options: Only the nightly report
Only the pre-merge check
Both, to halve the cost
Neither, because batches cannot process code
questions.explain:
Batches save 50% but may take up to 24 hours with no latency guarantee. A developer is waiting on the pre-merge check, so it stays synchronous.
Not “Only the pre-merge check” — A developer is blocked on the pre-merge check, and a batch can take up to 24 hours.
Not “Both, to halve the cost” — The saving is real, but the pre-merge check cannot wait for a batch window.
Not “Neither, because batches cannot process code” — Batches accept any message request, code included. The nightly report is an ideal fit.

questions.q: Claude generates a change and is then asked, in the same session, to review it. It reports no problems, and a subtle bug ships. What is the better design?
options: Review with an independent instance that lacks the generation context
Ask the same session to review twice
Add “be critical of your own work” to the prompt
Have the session rate its confidence and re-review below 7
questions.explain:
A session keeps the reasoning behind its own output and seldom challenges it. An independent reviewer catches more.
Not “Ask the same session to review twice” — The second pass has the same context and therefore the same blind spots.
Not “Add “be critical of your own work” to the prompt” — The instruction does not remove the reasoning the session is anchored on.
Not “Have the session rate its confidence and re-review below 7” — Self-rated confidence is unreliable, and the session is confident for the same reasons it missed the bug.

questions.q: After a long conversation is summarised, the agent tells the customer the refund is “about $80” when it was $84.37, and gets the order date wrong. What prevents this?
options: Keep amounts, dates and IDs in a persistent case-facts block outside the summary
Summarise more often with shorter summaries
Ask the summariser to be more careful with numbers
Raise max_tokens on each reply
questions.explain:
Progressive summarisation blurs exact values. Transactional facts need to live verbatim outside the summarised history.
Not “Summarise more often with shorter summaries” — Each summarising pass is another chance to blur the figures.
Not “Ask the summariser to be more careful with numbers” — It may help a little, but exact values kept only inside a summary can still be lost.
Not “Raise max_tokens on each reply” — Output length is not the cause. The exact values were lost from the input history.

questions.q: A customer opens with “I want to speak to a person”. The issue looks like one the agent could solve in a single step. What should the agent do?
options: Escalate straight away
Resolve the issue first, then offer a handoff
Ask why they want a person
Check sentiment before deciding
questions.explain:
An explicit request for a human is honoured immediately, without further investigation.
Not “Resolve the issue first, then offer a handoff” — That overrides a clear request. Offering to help first is right only when the customer has not asked for a person.
Not “Ask why they want a person” — It delays a request the customer has already made plainly.
Not “Check sentiment before deciding” — Sentiment is irrelevant here. The customer has said what they want.

questions.q: get_customer returns three accounts for the name “Priya Sharma”. What is the correct next step?
options: Ask the customer for another identifier, such as email or order number
Use the most recently active account
Use the account with an open order
Escalate to a human agent
questions.explain:
Several matches are resolved by asking, not by heuristics. This is within the agent’s scope, so escalation is premature.
Not “Use the most recently active account” — That is a guess. Acting on the wrong account could expose another customer’s data.
Not “Use the account with an open order” — Also a guess: more than one account may have an open order, or the issue may concern a closed one.
Not “Escalate to a human agent” — The agent can settle this itself with one question. Escalating wastes a person’s time.

questions.q: One of three research subagents hits a search timeout. What should the system do?
options: Retry locally; if it still fails, return a structured error with partial results, and note the gap in the report
Abort the whole run and report failure
Leave that subtopic out of the report without comment
Return an empty result so synthesis can continue
questions.explain:
Aborting everything and silent suppression are both anti-patterns. Local recovery, structured propagation and coverage annotation keep the report honest.
Not “Abort the whole run and report failure” — Two of the three subtopics succeeded. Aborting throws that work away.
Not “Leave that subtopic out of the report without comment” — Readers would take the report as complete. The gap has to be stated.
Not “Return an empty result so synthesis can continue” — Empty means “nothing found”, which is false here and would mislead the synthesis.

questions.q: The pipeline shows 97% accuracy overall and the team wants to drop human review. What should happen first?
options: Measure accuracy by document type and by field, using stratified sampling
Remove review, since 97% beats the target
Wait until the overall figure reaches 99%
Ask the model to rate its confidence on each document
questions.explain:
An aggregate figure can mask a segment that performs badly. Validate per type and per field before automating.
Not “Remove review, since 97% beats the target” — The overall figure could hide a document type or field that fails far more often.
Not “Wait until the overall figure reaches 99%” — A higher overall figure has the same blind spot.
Not “Ask the model to rate its confidence on each document” — Self-rated confidence has to be calibrated against labelled data before it can be trusted.

questions.q: Two sources give a market size of $4.2B (published 2023) and $5.1B (published 2025). How should the synthesis handle this?
options: Report both figures with their sources and dates
Use the more recent figure
Report the average
Drop the statistic as unreliable
questions.explain:
Conflicts are annotated with attribution, not resolved arbitrarily. The dates may show these are different points in time rather than a contradiction.
Not “Use the more recent figure” — Choosing one silently hides the other source, and the two may describe different years.
Not “Report the average” — An average is a number that no source reported.
Not “Drop the statistic as unreliable” — Dropping it loses useful information. Both figures are valid alongside their dates.

questions.q: Deep into a long investigation, the agent starts describing “typical patterns in such systems” rather than the classes it read earlier. What is the best response?
options: Save key findings to a scratchpad file and hand verbose exploration to subagents
Ask the same question again more firmly
Paste the full repository into the conversation
Raise max_tokens on the response
questions.explain:
This is context degradation. Persisting findings outside the context and isolating discovery output are the standard remedies.
Not “Ask the same question again more firmly” — The detail has already faded from the working context, so repeating the question gets the same drift.
Not “Paste the full repository into the conversation” — More input makes the context pressure worse.
Not “Raise max_tokens on the response” — max_tokens governs output length, not how well earlier input is retained.

questions.q: Contracts often carry amendments: the original clause sets payment at 30 days and Amendment 1 changes it to 45. The extraction returns one value or the other, with nothing to show which applies. What is the most effective fix?
options: Change the schema so an amended field holds every value, each with its source location and effective date
Tell the model in the prompt to always take the latest amendment and ignore the original terms
Run a classifier first that strips superseded sections out of the document
After extraction, pattern-match for amendments and send those documents to manual review
questions.explain:
A single-value field forces the model to pick silently between two values the document really contains. A schema that keeps each value with its source and effective date loses nothing, and downstream code decides which one applies.
Not “Tell the model in the prompt to always take the latest amendment an…” — A prompt rule is only probably followed, and the latest amendment is not always the one in force. The original value and its source are still lost.
Not “Run a classifier first that strips superseded sections out of the d…” — Deciding what is superseded is the hard part, and this hands it to a new model that can be wrong. Text it removes can never be recovered by the extraction, and amendments often change only part of a clause.
Not “After extraction, pattern-match for amendments and send those docum…” — This detects the problem without fixing it. Amendments are frequent, so most contracts would end up in manual review.

questions.q: After three months of full human review, extractions with model confidence above 90% show 97% accuracy overall. The team plans to stop reviewing those high-confidence extractions. Which check matters most before that goes live?
options: Break accuracy down by document type and by field, to confirm high-confidence extractions hold up in every segment and not only in aggregate
Compare accuracy at 85%, 90% and 95% confidence to find the cutoff that automates the most with the fewest errors
Run a two-week pilot that sends 25% of high-confidence extractions straight to downstream systems and watch the error reports
Confirm that 97% accuracy is enough for every downstream system that uses the data
questions.explain:
An overall figure can hide a weak segment: one document type could sit at 70% while the others are at 99%. Automating on the aggregate alone would let that segment through unreviewed.
Not “Compare accuracy at 85%, 90% and 95% confidence to find the cutoff …” — Tuning the cutoff still relies on an aggregate figure at each threshold. A segment that fails stays hidden at 95% just as it does at 90%.
Not “Run a two-week pilot that sends 25% of high-confidence extractions …” — A pilot finds the weak segment by letting real errors reach downstream systems. Three months of reviewed data can answer the question with no risk.
Not “Confirm that 97% accuracy is enough for every downstream system tha…” — A fair check, but it takes the 97% as true for every document. That figure is the thing not yet validated: one segment may sit far below it.

questions.q: A customer writes: “This is frustrating. I have explained my issue twice and nothing is resolved. I want a real person NOW.” The agent has not called any tool on their account yet. What should it do?
options: Call escalate_to_human straight away and pass the conversation history
Acknowledge the frustration and ask one targeted question about the issue before escalating
Explain briefly what the agent can help with and offer a quick fix, escalating only if the customer asks again
Call get_customer and lookup_order first to gather account context, then escalate
questions.explain:
The customer has asked for a person in plain words. An explicit request for a human is honoured at once, and the history goes with it so they do not have to explain a third time.
Not “Acknowledge the frustration and ask one targeted question about the…” — The customer has already explained twice and asked for a person. One more question delays a clear request.
Not “Explain briefly what the agent can help with and offer a quick fix,…” — This overrides what the customer asked for. Offering to help first fits only when they have not asked for a person.
Not “Call get_customer and lookup_order first to gather account cont…” — Looking things up first makes an angry customer wait for work nobody asked for. The human agent can pull the account; what they need from the agent is the conversation history.
